summary: Cap-de-Rabast (Pointe-Nord) light, north tip of Anticosti Island: a 22 m concrete octagonal tower, built 1917-1919, automated in 1980, still shows a seasonal light.

light.note: Operates seasonally (Coast Guard List of Lights, 'Seasonal'). Originally three white flashes at four-second intervals, then an eclipse of twelve seconds (LighthouseFriends).

structures.note: 72 ft base to vane (Heritage Character Statement); built 1917-1918 per the statement, 1919 per LighthouseFriends and Les amis des phares
Housed a diaphone that sounded two, two-and-a-half-second blasts (LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Grounds open; tower closed (LighthouseFriends). Reached by the island's main dirt road: at kilometre 19 turn north and drive 16 km. Not staffed.

stay.note: Overnight stays in the two former keepers' dwellings, offered by Pourvoirie Lac-Geneviève d'Anticosti

events.note: Tower built 1917-1918 by the Department of Marine and Fisheries (Heritage Character Statement); the Marine reports record the new tower in fiscal 1918-19
Station established 1919 with the other north-shore lights (LighthouseFriends; Les amis des phares)
Three north-shore light and fog alarm stations, Cap de Rabast included, 'now in permanent operation' (Deputy Minister, fiscal 1920-21)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Heritage Character Statement says the tower was built 1917-1918; the Marine reports show the erection begun in fiscal 1917-18, new towers erected in 1918-19, and the stations in permanent operation by fiscal 1920-21; LighthouseFriends and Les amis des phares give 1919. These are the same build read at different stages; the record's 1919 is supportable.

The sources disagree on the houses: LighthouseFriends says a double dwelling was built in 1918-1919 and later replaced by separate residences; the Heritage statement says the two dwellings date from the 1950s. Not resolved.

notes_for_editor: 1) Keepers come from LighthouseFriends only. The Canadian keeper tables in the local Marine report corpus are OCR-garbled and the names did not surface in a search; these should be checked against the Marine keeper lists or Library and Archives Canada before publication. 2) LighthouseFriends prints 'Léon Element' and 'Clophas' (broken accent); both are kept as printed, with notes. 3) The Heritage statement's designation sentence reads 'the lighttower at Cap de la Table' (a slip for Cap de Rabast). 4) LighthouseFriends attributes the 'permanent operation' sentence to its 1920 annual report; the text is in the Deputy Minister's report for the fiscal year 1920-21 (printed 1922, Sessional Paper No. 21). 5) The Heritage statement dates the two dwellings to the 1950s; LighthouseFriends dates a double dwelling to 1918-19. Unresolved. 6) Cartier's naming and the 'place of turning back' gloss rest on LighthouseFriends; Cartier's own narrative was not read. 7) The Parks Canada Directory of Federal Heritage Designations page (ID 3954) and the Quebec provincial heritage record (patrimoine-culturel.gouv.qc.ca) could not be read (navigation only), so the designation date of 1990 is LighthouseFriends' alone. 8) The French route page quote is rendered in English as a translation: 'turn north and drive 16 kilometres'. 9) The record's local unit (Minganie RCM) was not checked. 10) The record's coordinates (49.951617, -64.149348) match the Coast Guard list (49 57 05.8 N, 064 08 57.4 W) to within about 10 m: no correction. 11) No wreck or rescue at the station was found in the sources read. 12) The Marine reports' 1918-19 north-route passage describes one winter voyage of vessels through the ice (scan p. 48), not this station; the story uses it only for the general point that the north side was preferred, and says the passage was a winter voyage. 13) Fixed in the 2026-10-28 check: the opening no longer cites Les amis des phares (which gives 1919) for 1917-1918 dates, and the 1953 surf account now says 'over their knees' as the source does, not 'waist-deep'.
